satz: Costs are the only part of the return that is known in advance.
warum: Before costs, the average active return must equal the market return; after costs, it is necessarily lower. This follows from arithmetic alone and does not need to be proven empirically. In the EU, active equity funds cost 1.50% a year over a ten-year horizon, ETFs 0.31% (ESMA, period 2012-2021). Accordingly, the net return was 9.4% compared with 10.4% a year.
von: William Sharpe, The Arithmetic of Active Management (1991)

satz: Fees of 1.3 percentage points a year cost around a third of the final wealth over 30 years.
warum: At a gross return of 7%, €10,000 grows to around €72,000 after 30 years if the ongoing charges are 0.20%. With costs of 1.50%, it is only around €49,800. The difference of about €22,100 is due solely to the expense ratio, because it applies every year to the amount that has already been compounded. After 40 years, the gap grows to around 39% of the final wealth.
von: Illustrative calculation based on John C. Bogle

satz: For active funds, price is the best selection criterion.
warum: In the Morningstar Active/Passive Barometer (as of 30 June 2025), 27% of the cheapest active funds outperformed their passive counterparts over ten years, but only 15% of the most expensive. In the US Large Blend category, the figures were 15.4% versus 3.9%. In these data, costs are the only factor that reliably predicts success.

satz: Performance comes, performance goes. Fees never falter.
warum: In Buffett's bet from 2008 to 2017, a simple S&P 500 index fund with a total gain of 125.8% won against five funds of hedge funds, which achieved between 2.8% and 87.7%. The funds of funds held over 200 individual hedge funds and paid around 2.5% a year in fixed fees regardless of the result. Taken together, they trailed the index in nine of the ten years.

satz: Above all, compound interest needs undisturbed time.
warum: One US dollar invested in 1900 had grown in nominal terms by the end of 2025 to $124,854 in US equities, to $284 in long-term bonds and to $69 in the money market (Dimson/Marsh/Staunton). In real terms, $3,296 remains for equities. This result came about without cleverly chosen timing, solely through 126 years of interest on interest. Every interruption costs disproportionately, because it reduces the base for all later years.

satz: Calculate with the geometric return, never with the arithmetic average.
warum: From 1928 to 2025, the S&P 500 returned 11.86% a year on an arithmetic basis, but only 10.02% on a geometric basis. If you enter 11.9% in the compound interest calculator, you overestimate the final wealth after 30 years by more than 60%. As a rule of thumb, the geometric return is lower than the arithmetic return by about half the variance.

satz: The average return is a calculated figure, not a typical year.
warum: In 98 years of the S&P 500, the annual return was between 8% and 12% only four times, namely in 1968, 1993, 2004 and 2016. The best year was 1954 at plus 52.6%, the worst was 1931 at minus 43.8%. Around one calendar year in four ended with a loss.

satz: Inflation reduces purchasing power with a compounding effect.
warum: For the S&P 500, after US inflation of 3.0%, 6.8% a year remained in real terms from 1928 to 2025, instead of 10.0% in nominal terms. In Germany, the harmonised index of consumer prices rose by 8.7% in 2022 and by 6.0% in 2023. A portfolio with a nominal return of 5% therefore lost around 3.4% in real terms in 2022. Only the real return shows how purchasing power changes.

satz: Ten German shares concentrate the portfolio on a small market.
warum: Germany accounts for less than 2.4% of the MSCI World, the USA for 72.1% (as of 31 August 2026). A portfolio of DAX shares thus unwittingly limits itself to a small segment of the world market. The preference for domestic shares, known as home bias, is regularly mistaken for diversification because many positions look like diversification.

satz: Check the concentration even in broad indices.
warum: The ten largest shares made up 26.6% of the MSCI World (as of 31 August 2026) and 37.5% of the MSCI Emerging Markets, with TSMC alone accounting for 15.1%. In addition, the MSCI World contains only 23 developed markets and neither emerging markets nor small caps. A broad index fund is therefore often less diversified than its name suggests.

satz: Higher economic growth is no promise of returns.
warum: From 1900 to 2025, equities in developed markets returned 8.5% a year in US dollars, emerging markets only 6.9% (Dimson/Marsh/Staunton). From 2001 to 2025, emerging markets were ahead in euros at 7.52% versus 6.26%, but with volatility of 24.4% instead of 17.7%. This lead comes entirely from the years 2001 to 2007.

satz: Diversification reduces the risk of individual investments, but not market risk.
warum: The five funds of funds in the Buffett bet together held over 200 hedge funds and still achieved only 0.3% to 6.5% a year. The globally diversified MSCI World lost 53.6% in euros from May 2001 to March 2009. Diversification therefore protects against the bankruptcy of individual companies, but not against a bear market.

satz: Back and forth empties your pockets.
warum: Barber and Odean analysed the data of 66,465 US households from the years 1991 to 1996. The most active fifth earned a net 11.4% a year, the average household 16.4% and the market 17.9%. Before costs, frequent and infrequent traders hardly differed; the gap arises almost entirely from trading costs and spreads.
von: Stock market saying; supported by Barber/Odean (2000)

satz: Selling winners too early and holding losers too long is the most expensive behavioural mistake.
warum: In 10,000 securities accounts, Odean (1998) found that winning positions were realised with a probability of 14.8%, losing positions with only 9.8%. In the following year, the winners that had been sold earned on average 3.4 percentage points more than the losers that had been held. So on average, the hope that the losers would recover was not fulfilled.

satz: The problem usually lies in when investors buy, not in the fund.
warum: According to Morningstar's “Mind the Gap 2026”, the average invested dollar earned 8.7% a year in the decade to the end of 2025, while the funds themselves earned 9.9%. The gap widens with volatility, from 0.4 percentage points in the calmest fifth of funds to over 2.0 percentage points in the most volatile fifth. Among experts, the size of the gap is disputed, but not the fact that investors on average earn less than their funds.

satz: Looking at your portfolio less often is a measure against bad decisions.
warum: Empirically, losses weigh around twice as heavily as gains of the same size. The meta-analysis by Brown and colleagues (2024) of 607 estimates gives a factor of 1.955. The more often you look, the more often you see losses. Displays of daily performance and push notifications lead to such short evaluation periods. Fixed, infrequent dates for looking at the portfolio reduce the number of occasions that prompt decisions.

satz: After minus 50%, it takes plus 100% to break even.
warum: Percentage changes are multiplied, not added. Plus 50% and minus 50% therefore result in minus 25%, not zero. The DAX lost 72.7% from March 2000 to March 2003; around 270% was needed to make up the loss. Limiting losses is therefore mathematically more valuable than it seems intuitively.

satz: The equity return is the compensation for crash risk.
warum: Since 1928, the S&P 500 has had around 100 declines of at least 10%, so on average about one a year. For enduring these declines, investors received a premium of 6.65 percentage points a year over the money market from 1928 to 2025. Without the risk of interim losses, this premium would not exist.

satz: First rule out ruin, then optimise the return.
warum: In a multiplicative coin toss with plus 50% for heads and minus 40% for tails, the expected value is plus 5% per round. The time average, that is the average development of a single player over many rounds, is around minus 5%, by contrast. The average across many players therefore does not describe the path that an individual player experiences. Position size and avoiding ruin are therefore more important than the expected value.
von: Nassim Taleb; ergodicity economics according to Ole Peters

satz: “Shares always come back” applies to broad indices, not to a single country.
warum: The Nikkei 225 stood at 38,915.87 points on 29 December 1989 and did not reach a new all-time high until 22 February 2024, after 34 years and 2 months. The S&P 500, too, needed around 86 months after the dotcom peak and around 65 months after the 2007 peak to reach a new high. In addition, indices remove insolvent companies and add successful ones. Individual shares have no such renewal.

satz: Cheap is not a margin of safety.
warum: Graham's margin of safety is the distance from the estimated intrinsic value and not a price that merely looks low. For defensive investors, he required, among other things, a P/E ratio of at most 15 and a price-to-book ratio of at most 1.5. He allowed a higher price-to-book ratio with a correspondingly lower P/E ratio, as long as the product of the two ratios was at most 22.5. Without a judgement about the business, a share with a low P/E ratio is often a value trap.

satz: A share is only worth buying if the company is better than what is priced in.
warum: In second-level thinking, quality is only an advantage if the market underestimates it. The annual forecasts for the S&P 500 show how inaccurate the consensus is. From 2018 to 2025, the consensus estimate was within plus/minus 10 percentage points of the actual result in only one of eight years. For 2022, strategists expected plus 3.9%; the actual result was minus 19.4%.

satz: Profit only counts after deducting maintenance capital expenditure.
warum: Buffett's owner earnings are reported earnings plus non-cash items, less the capital expenditure needed to maintain competitive position and unit volume. See's Candies shows the difference. The company was bought in 1972 for $25 million and tied up only $8 million of capital. In 2007 it made a pre-tax profit of $82 million, for which an additional $32 million of capital had been invested since 1972. The third component, the capital expenditure, has to be estimated and does not appear in any financial statements.
von: Warren Buffett, appendix to the 1986 shareholder letter

satz: Returns are only comparable after costs and taxes.
warum: Index returns deduct neither fund costs nor custody fees, spreads, flat-rate withholding tax (Abgeltungsteuer) or the advance lump sum (Vorabpauschale). Between the index return and what actually arrives in the portfolio there can easily be 0.3 to 1.5 percentage points a year. Even the gap between the gross and net index of the MSCI World is around 0.55 percentage points a year. It arises from non-refundable withholding tax on dividends.

satz: Taxes belong in the calculation, but never justify an investment decision.
warum: Only in December do investors realise more losses (12.8%) than gains (10.8%); in the other eleven months it is the other way round (Odean 1998). Tax-efficient behaviour is therefore possible, but it is overridden by the disposition effect. Loss offsetting belongs in the annual plan. It justifies neither selling a good position nor holding on to a bad one.

satz: Without a sale, the tax is deferred, and the amount continues to earn a return.
warum: Through the tax that becomes due, every realised gain reduces the base on which compound interest works in the following years. How much this matters is shown by the arithmetic of costs, according to which 1.3 percentage points less a year cost around 31% of the final wealth over 30 years. At the average portfolio turnover of 75% a year that Barber and Odean measured, turnover has a double effect, namely through trading costs and through taxes paid earlier.

satz: Automation beats discipline.
warum: Johnson and Goldstein (2003) compared organ donation rates. In Germany, with an opt-in system, the rate was 12%; in Austria, with an opt-out system, it was 99.98%. In the online experiment, a single mouse click was enough to switch, yet 42% consented under opt-in and 82% under opt-out. With a savings plan, the decision is made once; after that, doing nothing is the default.

satz: The investment horizon determines the equity allocation, not the current market situation.
warum: Looking at 50 years of the DAX, 20-year investment periods returned 8.4% a year on average, 3.3% in the worst case and 15.2% in the best (DAX return triangle of the Deutsches Aktieninstitut, as of 31 December 2025). With a holding period of one year, the range ran from minus 43.9% to plus 84.1%. A longer holding period narrows the range but guarantees nothing, because overlapping time windows are not independent samples.

satz: An emergency fund is a prerequisite for staying the course and therefore not a bad investment.
warum: Investors who need money during a slump have to sell at the low. In euros, the MSCI World was at one point 53.6% below its high. Kostolany, who went bankrupt twice, derived from his own losses the rule never to buy shares on credit. For him, having your own money is the first of the four Gs (Geld, Gedanken, Geduld, Glück), alongside thoughts, patience and luck.

satz: Knowing about a cognitive bias does not protect you from it.
warum: The bias blind spot is itself a bias. Knowledge alone hardly changes behaviour, whereas rules and automatic routines do. In Asch's experiments, 74% of participants gave an obviously wrong answer at least once, only because the group gave it. When tested alone, the error rate was below 0.7%. What works is a written investment policy statement, a savings plan, a fixed rebalancing date and a decision journal.

satz: The purchase price is meaningless to the market.
warum: Anchors, that is starting values on which an estimate is based, have an effect even when they are apparently random. In Tversky and Kahneman (1974), after the wheel-of-fortune anchor 10, subjects estimated the percentage of African countries in the UN at a median of 25%, and after the anchor 65 at 45%. The wheel was set so that it only stopped at 10 or 65. The purchase price is the reference point most used by private investors and is meaningless for the future of a share. It is more useful to consider whether you would buy the position again today at this price.

satz: In a crisis, taking action feels right and is usually wrong.
warum: Bar-Eli and colleagues (2007) analysed 286 penalty kicks. Goalkeepers almost always dive to the left or right, because doing nothing looks worse after conceding a goal, even though staying put would be the best option. In a portfolio, the urge to at least do something is most expensive when doing nothing would be optimal. Rules set in advance replace the impulse with a plan.

satz: With every success statistic, check who is missing from it.
warum: Of the active US equity funds that existed 20 years ago, only 37.3% were still in existence at the end (SPIVA, as of 30 June 2025). Over ten years, the figure was 63.8%. The funds that were closed or merged were almost always the poor ones and do not appear in any ranking. Elton, Gruber and Blake put the resulting bias at 0.9 percentage points a year.

satz: The economy is the master, the stock market the dog on a long lead.
warum: With this image, Kostolany describes how prices can move far above or below the fundamentals in the short term but return to them in the long term. Individual decades show how large the deviations can become. In euros, the MSCI World returned 11.3% a year from 2016 to 2025, but minus 3.8% from 2000 to 2009. Both periods were exceptional phases.

satz: You cannot forecast the cycle, but you can assess where you currently stand.
warum: Marks separates forecasting from assessing where you stand. For him, the willingness to take risk depends on whether greed or fear currently prevails in the market. The annual estimates for the S&P 500 show that forecasts do not help here. In 2022 the consensus was 23.3 percentage points off, and in 2023 and 2024 it underestimated two years that each gained over 20%. Accordingly, Kostolany determines the market phase from trading volume and share ownership rather than from the price.
von: Howard Marks; phase theory according to André Kostolany

satz: Buying opportunities are only recognisable in hindsight.
warum: Bear markets end when the news is at its worst. On 9 March 2009 and 23 March 2020, this was only recognisable in hindsight. Around 76% of the best trading days fall in a bear market or in the first two months after it. For example, the S&P 500 rose by 9.5% on 9 April 2025, one day after the low. The index fund in the Buffett bet fell from 100 to 63 in 2008 and stood at 225.8 at the end of 2017.
